title: The Governor's Midnight Report and the Floor Test Rule
hook: After a state government was dismissed overnight without a legislative vote, a nine-judge Constitution Bench rewrote the limits of President's Rule.
laws: Constitution of India (Article 74, Article 355, and Article 356)

facts.label: Court
facts.value: Supreme Court of India (Nine-Judge Constitution Bench)

facts.label: Triggering Event
facts.value: Dismissal of the Karnataka ministry and dissolution of the 224-member Assembly on April 21, 1989 without a floor test

facts.label: Consolidated Matters
facts.value: Challenges to Article 356 proclamations in Karnataka, Meghalaya, Nagaland, and four states dismissed in December 1992

facts.label: Outcome
facts.value: Nine-judge bench held Article 356 proclamations are judicially reviewable and made the Assembly floor test mandatory

summary: In April 1989, nineteen legislators handed withdrawal letters to the Karnataka Governor, though seven retracted through affidavits within twenty-four hours and the cabinet asked for an Assembly floor test. Refusing a vote on the house floor, the Governor sent a report recommending President's Rule, and on April 21, 1989 the President dismissed the government and dissolved the 224-member legislature.

After the Karnataka High Court dismissed the challenge in June 1989, the appeal was heard alongside similar dismissals in Meghalaya and Nagaland as well as the December 1992 dismissals of four state governments following the Ayodhya demolition. On March 11, 1994, a nine-judge Constitution Bench delivered a landmark judgment curbing arbitrary use of Article 356.

The bench held that while Article 74(2) bars courts from inspecting ministerial advice itself, the President's satisfaction and the underlying Governor's report remain open to judicial review for mala fides or absence of relevant material. Ruling that a government's majority must be tested only on the floor of the Assembly and that legislatures cannot be dissolved before parliamentary approval, the court struck down the Karnataka, Meghalaya, and Nagaland dismissals while upholding the 1992 proclamations on the ground that secularism is part of the Constitution's Basic Structure.

judgment.outcome: Proclamations in Karnataka, Meghalaya, and Nagaland declared unconstitutional (without restoring expired terms); December 1992 proclamations in four states upheld as valid measures to protect secularism.
points: Presidential proclamations under Article 356 are not immune from judicial review; courts may strike them down if issued mala fide or based on wholly extraneous or irrelevant material.
Article 74(2) bars inquiry into the advice tendered by the Council of Ministers to the President, not into the factual material and Governor's report underlying that advice.
The floor of the Legislative Assembly is the sole democratic forum to decide whether a ministry enjoys majority support, barring exceptional cases of all-pervasive violence.

A state assembly may only be placed in suspended animation—never dissolved—until both Houses of Parliament approve the Article 356 proclamation within two months, and courts retain power to restore a wrongly dismissed government.

principles.name: Judicial Review of Emergency Proclamations
principles.meaning: Executive satisfaction under Article 356 is conditional and reviewable to verify whether relevant material existed to show a constitutional breakdown.
principles.inThisCase: The court examined the Governor's report in Karnataka and found that bypassing an available floor test rendered the dismissal unconstitutional.

principles.name: Primacy of the Legislative Floor Test
principles.meaning: A Governor cannot privately count heads at Raj Bhavan when the legislature is available to vote on confidence.
principles.inThisCase: The nine-judge bench held that conflicting affidavits outside the house could only be resolved through a floor test in the Assembly.

principles.name: Secularism as Part of the Basic Structure
principles.meaning: Federalism and secularism are foundational features of the Constitution that bind all state governments.
principles.inThisCase: The bench upheld the December 1992 dismissals in four states because acts undermining secularism constitute a failure of constitutional machinery.

takeaways: Majority support for a state government must be tested on the Assembly floor, not in the Governor's chamber.
President's Rule is subject to judicial review and cannot be used to dissolve a legislature before Parliament approves the proclamation.
Secularism is an unamendable constitutional principle whose breach can justify central intervention.

social.hook: Can a state government be dismissed overnight without ever facing a vote in the Assembly?
social.script: Can a state government be dismissed overnight without ever facing a vote in the Assembly? In April 1989, nineteen legislators handed withdrawal letters to the Karnataka Governor, though seven retracted within twenty-four hours. Refusing the cabinet's request for a floor test, the Governor recommended President's Rule, and the 224-member Assembly was dissolved on April 21, 1989. Five years later, on March 11, 1994, a nine-judge Constitution Bench transformed Indian federalism. It ruled that Article 356 proclamations are open to judicial review, made the Assembly floor test the sole measure of majority, barred dissolution before parliamentary approval, and affirmed secularism as Basic Structure. You be the judge. Full case notes are on the Courtroom Chronicles website.

carousel.heading: The 1989 Midnight Dismissal
carousel.text: Despite seven legislators retracting withdrawal letters, the Karnataka government was dismissed without a legislative floor test.

carousel.heading: The High Court Rejection
carousel.text: The Karnataka High Court dismissed the challenge, leading to consolidated appeals before a nine-judge Constitution Bench.

carousel.heading: The Constitutional Question
carousel.text: Are Article 356 proclamations immune from judicial review, or can courts examine the Governor's report?

carousel.heading: The Nine-Judge Mandate
carousel.text: On March 11, 1994, the bench ruled that floor tests are mandatory and assemblies cannot be dissolved before parliamentary approval.

carousel.heading: Why It Matters
carousel.text: The ruling curbed arbitrary central takeovers and cemented secularism and federalism as unshakeable constitutional pillars.
